HEIKE SCHROEDER1*, HEATHER LOVELL2
1Environmental Change Institute, University of Oxford, South Parks Road, Oxford OX1 3QY, UK 2School of Geosciences, University of Edinburgh, Drummond Street, Edinburgh EH8 9XP, UK

United Nations climate change conferences have attracted an increasing number and range of observer participants, often outnumbering national delegates. The interactions between the formal and informal spaces of climate governance at the Conference of the Parties (COP) are explored by investigating why non-nation state actors (NNSAs) attend them and by measuring to what extent ofﬁcial UN Side Events provide relevant information for the formal negotiations. Based on primary empirical research at recent COPs, it is found that 60–75% of Side Events have related directly to items under negotiation in the post-2012 climate negotiations. In this regard, Side Events that facilitate informal exchange between stakeholders not only provide input into the negotiations but also allow issues beyond the realm of the negotiations to be discussed, reﬂecting the scope of climate change. Although Side Events are an effective forum to exchange ideas and network, their current format and purpose as being events ‘on the side’ does not offer a sufﬁcient framework for coordination between the work of NNSAs and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) process.
Keywords: climate change politics; Conference of the Parties (COP); international negotiations; non-nation state actors (NNSAs); Side Events; UNFCCC

1. Introduction

There is growing interest in the role of non-nation state actors (NNSAs) in governing climate change. Less has been written about the role of NNSAs at one particular event – the annual session of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) Conference of the Parties (COP). A notable exception is the work of Hjerpe et al. (2008) and Hjerpe and Linne´r (2010) on the functions of Side Events and the constituencies that attend them. The COP is the authoritative body of the UNFCCC and is mandated to periodically examine the obligations of the Parties and the institutional arrangements under the Convention and to promote and facilitate the exchange of information on measures to address climate change (UN, 1992, Article 7.2).

There has, in recent years, been a dramatic increase in attendance at the COPs by NNSAs, as demonstrated in Figure 1, which shows that – together with the almost universal participation of nation-states – nearly 1,400 non-governmental and intergovernmental organizations had observer status under the UNFCCC at the 2009 COP 15 held in Copenhagen. This is up from just over 1,000 such organizations the previous year and is over eight times as high as at COP 1 in 1995. Before 2010, each registered observer organization was able to nominate any number of representatives to attend, but in 2010, for the ﬁrst time, observer organizations were given a quota. Until 2010 there had been no upper limit on the number of observer organizations admitted by the UNFCCC at any given time. Figure 2 shows the signiﬁcant increase in the number of observers compared to national delegates attending the COPs (which have also increased over time, most dramatically at COP 15). It is indeed striking that observers have outnumbered delegates at the majority of COP meetings, and many national delegations also admit non-governmental organization (NGO), municipal or business representatives into their delegations, raising the total number even further. At COP 15 in 2009, the number of media, NGO and intergovernmental observer organization delegates registered reached a record ﬁgure of 16,700 (compared to 10,600 country delegates), prompting controversial moves by the UNFCCC to signiﬁcantly restrict observer organization entry in the ﬁnal week of the COP due to space restrictions (Fisher, 2010).

This article explores the interactions between the formal (international negotiations) and informal (observer attendance, Side Events, etc.) spaces of climate governance at the COP. Speciﬁcally, it examines why NNSAs are attending the COP in increasing numbers, and measures to what extent Side Events speak to (i.e. provide relevant information for) the formal UNFCCC negotiations, based on

research conducted jointly by the authors (with assistance from a team at the Environmental Change Institute, University of Oxford) at COP 13 (2007, Bali), at COP 14 (2008, Poznan) and, with limitations, at COP 15 (2009, Copenhagen). Side Events are a platform for parties and intergovernmental and civil society organizations to present and discuss their work on key issues related to climate change, alongside the negotiations. The research demonstrates how the COP is an important – and theoretically relatively neglected – annual focal point for NNSA climate mitigation and adaptation activities, and indicates the range of NNSA perspectives, interests and framings of climate change in an unprecedented way.

The article is structured as follows. In Section 2, a conceptual framework on climate change governance at and beyond the COP is provided. Side Events (and the more recent emergence of Parallel Events) as ways in which NNSAs can provide relevant information on items under negotiation at the COP are also discussed. In Section 3 the research design is explained, and in Section 4 the ﬁndings of the survey, interviews, commentaries and participant observations on NNSA attendance at the COP and Side Events are presented and discussed. In Section 5, ﬁve conclusions are drawn on the way that the interaction between the formal and informal spaces at the COP is developing.
2. Conceptualizing NNSA climate governance at UN climate meetings

The climate change governance literature increasingly recognizes that NNSAs are visible and inﬂuential forces in the international climate regime and beyond (Auer, 2000; Newell, 2000; Betsill and Bulkeley, 2004, 2006; Gulbrandsen and Andresen, 2004; Betsill and Corell, 2008; Gaventa, 2009; Okereke et al., 2009). Parallel climate initiatives by NNSAs have grown at all levels of governance and encompass a wide variety of actors, ranging from small community groups to large multinational corporations. Their actions on climate change may have a material impact on the reduction of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and on the international climate negotiation process. According to Betsill and Corell (2008, p. 2), international negotiations cannot be understood merely as processes among national governments, but as involving ‘myriad actors representing a diversity of interests’. The COP has gained the status of ‘environmental mega-conferences’, ‘not because of the ofﬁcial agreements reached, but because they help set global agendas, facilitate “joined-up” thinking and
provide global leadership for national and local governments’ (Gaventa, 2009, p. 39; see also Seyfang and Jordan, 2002; Jordan and O’Riordan, 2003; Seyfang, 2003).

The literature on global governance has drawn attention to the multitude of actors who inﬂuence how climate change is addressed. Here, nation-states are generally seen as having the ultimate or sovereign authority, with NNSAs inﬂuencing state actors rather than exercising agency in their own right (Auer, 2000; Betsill and Bulkeley, 2004). While this may be true in the international climate negotiations, examples abound where NNSAs are acting authoritatively and in their own right in the informal climate arena beyond the formal UNFCCC regime (see e.g. Okereke, 2007; Burch, 2009; Schroeder and Bulkeley, 2009).

In the UNFCCC, negotiations toward a post-2012 agreement started in Bali in 2007 at COP 13, where the Bali Action Plan launched a two-year negotiating process. COP 15 in 2009 (Copenhagen) failed to reach agreement and instead took note of the Copenhagen Accord and extended negotiations beyond 2009 (Dimitrov, 2010). Since 2007, several issues have received increased attention in the negotiations, including adaptation and reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation (REDD). These issues have each brought a signiﬁcant pool of expertise and experience from NNSAs into the negotiations (Liverman and Billett, 2010; Schroeder, 2010).

The study here builds on this conceptualization of the COP as a mega-conference where global agendas are set, thinking is joined-up and leadership emerges (Gaventa, 2009) by looking speciﬁcally at the role of NNSAs at the COP meetings and the Side Events. This is a surprisingly under-researched area, given the increasing popularity of the COP, with NNSAs attending in ever-greater numbers. The work of Hjerpe et al. provides a rare example of COP Side Event research within political science. A survey by Hjerpe et al. (2008) on COP 13 and COP 14 Side Events summarized the six main functions of Side Events as: (i) building capacity; (ii) introducing potential items for negotiations; (iii) interconnecting people and policy areas; (iv) disseminating information; (v) providing a forum for other levels of governance; and (vi) legitimizing global governance. Their research also revealed that about a quarter of Side Event attendees are negotiators or government representatives, mostly from the G77 and China. Hjerpe et al. (2008) conclude importantly that the Side Events are not just a ‘parallel world’ with little interaction with the formal negotiating sessions, but instead they have a valuable capacity-building function. Every year, a large number of participants attend the COP for the ﬁrst time and use Side Events as a way to educate themselves about pertinent issues associated with climate change (Hjerpe et al., 2008; Hjerpe and Linne´r, 2010).

Building on the research of Hjerpe et al. (2008) and Hjerpe and Linne´r (2010), the research presented here focuses more closely on questions about what NNSAs are hoping to achieve at the COP and what precisely they do while they are there. Furthermore, the article examines the topics of discussion at the Side Events, and the links drawn (or not) to the negotiations. Before turning in detail to consider these questions, however, aspects of the UNFCCC meetings are brieﬂy introduced and the role of Side Events outlined.

The UNFCCC recognizes the value of NNSAs actively participating in the COP in that they bring ‘vital experience, expertise, information and perspectives . . . into the process to generate new insights and approaches’ (UNFCCC, 2003, p. 3). In addition, the ofﬁcial UNFCCC guidelines for the participation of NNSAs emphasize that ‘the access and participation of observers to the process promotes transparency in this increasingly complex universal problem’ (UNFCCC, 2003). Historically, NNSA participation and Side Events in the climate regime emerged from a broader push towards greater NGO involvement, which was precipitated largely by the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and its parallel NGO forum. Similar practices have emerged in the other Rio Conventions, although informal activities (i.e. observer participation and organizing Side Events) have been especially prevalent in the UNFCCC.

There are a number of activities that observer organizations can undertake at the COP, including observing the ofﬁcial negotiations (where permitted, as some sessions have restricted access), organizing and participating in Side Events (and Parallel Events), hosting exhibits, holding meetings and informal discussions at the numerous social events, making statements in plenary meetings, submitting written proposals (the latter two forms of engagement are, however, heavily restricted), holding press conferences and engaging in protests or advocacy.

One important way in which NNSAs are engaging in the climate convention process is through so-called ‘constituencies’. Constituencies are loose groups of like-minded organizations, somewhat similar in nature to the negotiating coalitions that have been formed by countries. The secretariat interacts with constituency chairs or focal points. They currently include the Business and Industry Non-Governmental Organizations and the Environmental Non-Governmental Organizations, both formed in 1992, the Local Government and Municipal Authorities formed in 1995, the Indigenous Peoples’ Organizations formed in 2001, the Research and Independent Non-Governmental Organizations formed in 2003, and the Trade Union Non-Governmental Organizations formed in 2008. The constituency focal points facilitate the exchange of information between the secretariat and the admitted observer organizations. Some groups such as faith groups and parliamentarians are currently not organized into constituencies.

Side Events and exhibits were originally established by the UNFCCC Secretariat as a forum for observer organizations to highlight diverse climate change-related issues in an environment separate from the negotiation process itself. Side Events are usually held in the form of panel discussions on a common theme, featuring presenters from different organizations or a single Party or intergovernmental or non-governmental organizations. They can also take the form of presentations and workshops. Some Side Event organizers invite discussants, which may represent different constituencies, to provide their perspectives or feedback. Side Events usually end with a question-and-answer session to engage the audience.

The UNFCCC Secretariat administers the Side Events. It selects them mainly based on relevance and a ﬁrst-come, ﬁrst-served basis, except for Parties, who are guaranteed a slot if they wish to have one, and allocates time slots and rooms free of charge. The 1.5- or 2-hour sessions were, until recently, timed to coincide with breaks in the formal negotiations, but have now expanded into formal negotiation times. After receiving a record 351 applications for 181 available slots for Side Events at COP 14 in 2008, this ﬁgure was surpassed at COP 15 in 2009 with 517 applications for an initial 136 slots. The UNFCCC Secretariat subsequently increased this to 255 slots to accommodate the increase in demand, but due to cancellations in the last few days of COP 15 only 217 took place. At COP 16, 249 Side Events were held and about 400 applications were submitted (Hjerpe and Linne´r, 2010, p. 14; UNFCCC, 2010, p. 8; informal consultations). There is a peak in the number of Side Events around the middle weekend of the 2-week COP; this pattern is reﬂected in Figure 3, showing the number of Side Events held per day at COP 14.

Although Side Events were held in a different venue to the formal sessions at COP 13 in Bali, and again at COP 16 in Cancun (requiring taking a shuttle back and forth) and were thereby perceived more strongly as a different ‘universe’ (Lovell, 2007), they were in closer geographical proximity in Poznan and Copenhagen.

While there are evidently several types of engagement, the ofﬁcial UN Side Events at the COP are arguably the most prominent. Side Events provide a forum for interaction among national delegates, intergovernmental and observer organization representatives, and the media. A selection of Side Events is covered daily by a publication called the Earth Negotiations Bulletin on the Side, a service provided by the International Institute of Sustainable Development (IISD). Although they cannot yet be broadcast on the Internet, organizers can make material, such as slides, available on the UNFCCC website.

Based on observations and data, the research here suggests that the role and scope of Side Events has changed over time. Informal conversations and interviews with people with responsibility in the UNFCCC Secretariat for organizing Side Events revealed how the UNFCCC Secretariat struggles to manage the growing interest among delegations, intergovernmental organizations and NGOs in organizing Side Events given limited space and resources. The Secretariat gravitates between being a clearing house for any kind of information relating to climate change, and a more carefully screened selection of relevant and quality information relating more narrowly to the UNFCCC process. Hjerpe et al. (2008) suggest further upgrading civil society input into the UNFCCC process by increasing reporting on Side Events and channelling information and insights into the formal sessions.

NNSAs can also organize and participate in the so-called Parallel Events. These are special-interest events that are organized outside of the ofﬁcial remit of the UNFCCC, but during the same time as the COP and usually during the middle weekend of the 2-week conference. It is not required to have a COP attendee badge to participate in Parallel Events. Examples are Forest Day, Climate & Development Days and Business Day, which bring together different stakeholders and foster information exchange and dialogue through plenary talks, parallel sessions, informal dialogue and exhibits. Parallel Events have become increasingly popular, with a signiﬁcant number taking place alongside the ofﬁcial sessions of the COP and its various bodies. There are several reasons to be cautious about the survey data. In particular, Side Event attendance was affected by a range of non-content factors such as the time of day, availability of refreshments and other concurrent events being timetabled. For this reason, the survey was complemented with more qualitative research methods. This included conducting 10 interviews with NNSA representatives about what they were doing at the COP and why they attended, an interview with a member of the UNFCCC Secretariat, several informal discussions, participant observation at key events hosted at or alongside the COP (e.g. Business Day in Bali), eight written commentaries by researchers attending COP 14 from the Environmental Change Institute, University of Oxford and the Tyndall Centre for

All interview quotes have been selected as representative of ﬁndings from the full set of interviews, which although exploratory are nevertheless judged here to be worthwhile reporting due to the limited empirical research in this ﬁeld to date.

The survey could not be continued at COP 15 as planned because of a logistical breakdown during the second week of the conference, which led to the cancellation of Side Events and, more problematically, few observer organizations gaining entry to the main conference venue. The UNFCCC Secretariat received over 40,000 nominations – and provided on-site registration for around 27,300 – for a conference venue with a capacity of 15,000. The number of civil society representatives allowed access on Tuesday and Wednesday of Week 2 was 7,000 and on the Thursday and Friday only 300. Although some Side Event organizers were able to ﬁnd alternative venues for their events, others cancelled their Side Events because of uncertainty about speakers getting inside the conference venue, or not even being able to register. COP 15 turned out to be an anomaly with regard to civil society involvement. Because the researchers involved in this study were themselves affected by the restriction of access to the conference venue (and so could not obtain a representative set of data), it was decided to limit the survey to COP 13 and COP 14.

4. Results and analysis

This section explores the interactions between the formal and informal arenas of climate governance at the COP. It examines two key questions. First, why do NNSAs attend the COP and Side Events? Second, to what extent do Side Events speak to the formal UNFCCC negotiations? These questions are answered using a mix of quantitative and qualitative data from COP 13 (Bali) and COP 14 (Poznan).

4.1. Why do NNSAs attend COPs and Side Events? The interviews and participant observations revealed a number of reasons for attending the COP and, in particular, Side Events. First, it was clear that NNSAs felt there was a different dynamic to the formal UNFCCC negotiations and the Side Events. The Side Events were seen by interviewees as ‘solutions-focused’, with vigorous debate about new ideas for mitigating climate change, as well as presentations of the latest climate science. The negotiations, on the other hand, were seen as revolving around negotiating skills, vested interests and political power, as one interviewee commented:

Any international agreement is like a 180-piece puzzle, because you have to get 180 countries to agree. It is always watered down from what we actually need to tackle climate change . . . it will always be behind the science (NNSA – Director of Policy & Regulation, Bali COP, December 2007).

The majority of NNSAs interviewed perceived themselves and other NNSAs as quicker and more effective at dealing with climate change than nation-states. In the second week of both COP 13 and COP 14, when progress with the negotiations appeared to have stalled, NNSAs, as well as national governments at the Side Events, became increasingly vocal about the need for action on climate change. Their argument was that if stringent GHG targets were not going to emerge through the international regime then action should be taken using other avenues, that is, through business initiatives, partnerships between local authorities and so on, all topics of discussion prevalent at the Side Events.
Following on from this, the second ﬁnding from the interviews and participant observation was that some NNSAs evidently use the COP as a convenient location for discussions and meetings with other

NNSAs. For example, Business Day, a Parallel Event organized by the World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD), was speciﬁcally for business-to-business discussions. As the Director of the WBCSD explained, ‘we don’t have a good voice at the COP and wanted to organize a speciﬁc day’ (Interview, December 2007). For many non-state actors the value of the COP is the convenience of having over 10,000 people working on climate science and policy in one place at the same time; it is a huge networking opportunity. In this sense, it is the formal UN climate negotiations that are a ‘side event’: they are not necessarily directly relevant to NNSAs except as a way of bringing the large international community of people working on climate change together. It is also noteworthy that at COP 13 and COP 14 a lot of businesses and NGOs left the COP before it ﬁnished.

Several interviewees identiﬁed that key reasons for NNSAs attending the COP are to be visible and to raise their proﬁle: it is ﬁrst and foremost a networking opportunity. As one interviewee explained in the aftermath of Bali, when asked about his reasons for attending:

However, the COP is not always an effective venue for NNSAs. Although the large majority of NNSAs that were interviewed see the COP as a worthwhile event, some concerns were voiced about the limited participation of the private sector. For example, as discussed, businesses are not directly able to obtain a pass to attend the COP according to UN rules, because observers have to have a non-proﬁt status and share the UNFCCC mission of mitigating climate change (which businesses do not). But business attendees can easily secure passes through other routes, typically trade associations.

When asked about how businesses seek to inﬂuence the negotiations and decision-making at the COP, one interviewee replied, ‘it is all pretty much informal chats . . . unfortunately there is no formal channel for the private sector to voice their concerns directly to the president of the COP’. This interviewee was not aware that the COP President, Executive Secretary, and other Chairpersons hold at least one meeting during every COP with the main observer constituencies. Observers can also always write to the COP President with concerns, as many of them do.

On a practical matter, interviewees also commented how it can be difﬁcult to organize meetings and co-ordinate staff, which relates in part to the informal nature of COP activities and to the growing size of the COP itself. For instance, one interviewee suggested that attending Side Events might not be the most efﬁcient use of resources for their company, explaining that ‘Side Events are one avenue where we want to inﬂuence, where we want to be present and to learn . . . but I know the network, I know the people, it would be just as efﬁcient to have a few staff with clear messages going to the individual people who are key players’. Further, for many NNSAs, international climate policy is just one focus of their activity; work in mitigating climate change takes place year-round across a range of private and public arenas.

The question is to what degree NNSA ideas, suggestions and knowledge are exchanged between informal observer activities and the formal negotiations, whether through protests by NGOs, observers lobbying national delegation leaders, Side Events attended by national delegation members, or through statements by constituencies. Although some negotiators and government representatives are actively attending Side Events (according to Hjerpe et al. (2008), 25% of Side Event attendees

belong in this category), the interaction appears (based on observation, interview ﬁndings and informal conversations) to be quite limited. NNSAs (NGOs and industry associations, but especially businesses and local governments) apply important pressure on governments, but there are practical limits to how effective they can be during the negotiations. Indeed, much of their inﬂuence on the negotiations may happen before and not actually at the COP.

4.2. To what extent do Side Events speak to the formal UNFCCC negotiations? The second part of the research focused on whether and, if so, how Side Events referred to the formal negotiations. The survey questions also covered the main topics addressed in the Side Events and levels of attendance. It was found that an unexpectedly high proportion of Side Events did not directly refer to the UN negotiations– 41% at COP 13 and 26% at COP 14, of which 18% at COP 13 and 10% at COP 14 indirectly referred to them (Figure 5). Examples of indirect reference include a Side Event on cities and climate change, where speakers critiqued that the UNFCCC was not paying enough attention to cities; a Side Event on the Growing Forests Partnership at the country level, which was implicitly embedded in the context of REDD; and a Side Event on how businesses might best respond post-2012. Examples of Side Events where there was no reference at all to the UNFCCC include one on the EU’s strategy to meet its 20/20/20 commitments, the role of renewable energy in meeting these commitments, the required acceleration of technology deployment and the role of wind energy; a Side Event focused on the relationship between disaster reduction and adaptation to climate change, the role of insurance and the success of Bangladesh in disaster reduction; and a Side Event covering the issues of ﬁnding a common language for addressing climate change, climate observation capacity, farmers’ participation and the adaptation capacity of ecosystems.

Given that Side Events are aimed at informing and feeding into the UN negotiations this is a surprising result. More reference to the UNFCCC negotiations was made at COP 14 in Poznan, and this is to be expected given the greater proximity to the signiﬁcant round of post-2012 negotiations at COP 15. This illustrates the multilevel nature of climate change and, moreover, how some aspects that are discussed in the Side Events are primarily national and local in nature and may or may not relate to the international negotiations, as argued by Hjerpe and Linne´r (2010). Side Events can function so as to provide a forum for other levels of governance. In other cases, issues may be discussed that are not yet on the international agenda, Hjerpe and Linne´r (2010) argue that Side Events both provide a forum for other levels of governance and introduce potential items for negotiation. This is consistent with Depledge (2005), who ﬁnds that Side Events are forums where issues that are too sensitive or political for the formal negotiations to discuss rationally are taken up. The survey results show that factors, such as the type of actor responsible for organizing the Side Event, and the international versus domestic relevance of the topic being addressed, clearly play a role in determining the level of interaction between the formal and informal spaces at the COP. There was no signiﬁcant difference in the popularity of negotiation-relevant versus not relevant Side Events. At COP 13, the average size of Side Events included in the survey that directly addressed the negotiations was 99; those that indirectly addressed them totalled 98, and those that did not address them at all, 72. For COP 14 the respective ﬁgures were 78, 71 and 85.

The survey data also revealed the particular aspects of the negotiations that were referred to in the Side Events where they were discussed. These data are shown in Figure 6. In Bali, at COP 13, the issue of REDD was most commonly raised with reference to the negotiations. Inter-estingly, in Poznan at COP 14, it was the nature of the negotiation process itself that was most discussed.

The survey results show that there are close linkages between Side Events and the negotiations, at least on certain topics. The best example here may be REDD, which was a key issue at Bali. This is as one might expect given both that COP 13 was held in Indonesia, a country for which REDD is a key negotiating issue, and also that the issue was in the agenda setting phase, a phase that is most conducive for input from NNSAs (Litﬁn, 1994; Cash, 2001; Guston, 2001; Schroeder et al., 2008). REDD was also a key issue at Poznan, which conﬁrms the high level of interest this issue continues to receive as the design of the REDD mechanism is being developed and negotiated (Young, 2008). It is also noteworthy that the Parallel Event Forest Day consistently had the highest level of attendance among Parallel Events (Figure 4). Attention on questions of architecture and process was strong in Poznan, a time when these essential questions remained unclear (Santarius et al., 2009). Understanding when and how ideas, frames and approaches emerging in the Side Events get diffused into the negotiations is a rich but, to date, understudied avenue of research.
5. Conclusions
The high degree of interest on the part of NNSAs in the UNFCCC process can be explained not just in terms of interest in the negotiations themselves but, importantly, in terms of bringing the growing

international community of people working on climate change together in one place. NNSAs engage in networking, holding meetings among peers, ﬁnding quick and effective solutions, debating new ideas and approaches and presenting novel research ﬁndings. The argument of many NNSAs is that if stringent GHG targets are not going to emerge through the international regime, then it is all the more important that action using other avenues is taken. This can be through business initiatives and partnerships among local authorities, which have been topics of discussion prevalent at the Side Events.

This research during the post-2012 climate negotiations ﬁnds that the interactions between the formal and informal arenas at the COP are quite varied; just under 60% of Side Events at COP 13 and 75% at COP 14 made frequent or direct reference to the negotiation process, while others were seemingly unrelated to the formal processes of the COP. Factors such as the type of actor responsible for organizing the Side Events, and the international versus domestic relevance of the topic being addressed, clearly play a role in determining the level of interaction between the formal and informal spaces at the COP. However, there were also many Side Events in this category that were entirely focused on the central issues in the negotiation process, such as the Clean Development Mechanism, REDD, adaptation, ﬁnancing, technology transfer and so on.

The results from this study clearly highlight that not all Side Events aim directly at the negotiations but, rather, that they represent a sliding scale of relevance to the UNFCCC and are, to some extent, also forums in and of themselves. The six functions of Side Events identiﬁed by Hjerpe and Linne´r (2010) can be associated with this variance in objectives, where ‘building capacity’ and ‘introducing potential items for negotiation’ have a strong relevance for the UNFCCC; ‘disseminating information’ and ‘interconnecting people and policy areas’ may have direct or indirect relevance; and ‘providing a forum for other levels of governance’ and ‘legitimizing global governance’ may not at all relate to the current negotiations but rather aim to raise the proﬁle of climate mitigation and adaptation activities ‘beyond the regime’ (Okereke et al., 2009). In addition, topics discussed in the Side Events that are not directly relevant to the negotiations can also represent new issues that have yet to be discussed in the negotiations. This question to what extent Side Events are a breeding ground for new ideas, which may eventually get introduced into the formal negotiations, is an important but under-studied area of research.

Questions regarding the ‘value added’ of the COP for NNSAs, and what could be done to strengthen it, need to be openly discussed and evaluated. Side Events clearly facilitate informal exchange between delegates, academics, business and civil society. In particular, the Side Events where delegates spoke were regarded as especially valuable by interviewees, as they produced the greatest level of debate and most provocative questions and responses. The same can be said for the more recent phenomenon of Parallel Events.

As currently structured, Side Events do not offer a framework to build a coordinated agenda between the work of NNSAs and the UNFCCC process. As the scope and prominence of climate change and the COP has grown, Side Events – in the traditional sense of being events on the side – are no longer ﬁt for purpose. The increasing impacts associated with climate change will incentivize more and more NNSAs to take actions to mitigate or adapt to climate change. The UNFCCC needs to look for innovative ways of how to integrate NNSAs more actively into the climate change regime.

To further strengthen this exchange and debate among stakeholders, future COP could group Side Events together to create large presenting blocks to facilitate communication among presenters of related approaches. This would resemble the format of the increasingly popular Parallel Events, where days are organized around certain themes, such as forests, oceans, development or business. It would create a rich learning environment for those able to attend a series of Side Events, offering a unique opportunity to gather all the latest thinking on a topic and bring together policymakers, practitioners, entrepreneurs and academics. It would also beneﬁt people who attend the COP for shorter

periods and primarily to follow certain issue areas. These suggestions on strengthening the exchange among different stakeholders have recently been implemented to some extent by way of the UN Secretariat encouraging organizers of Side Events with similar topics to merge them in order for them to be prioritized in the selection process. This was an attempt to manage the high number of applications for Side Events since COP 15, which amounted to approximately twice the available slots. A recent Stakeholder Dialogue report (Stakeholder Forum, 2010) conﬁrms these suggestions. The report recommends clustering Side Events according to the core building blocks in the negotiations, which are currently mitigation, adaptation, ﬁnance and technology transfer. It also proposes providing full and reliable Internet access in Side Event rooms to enable live broadcasting of Side Events and to allow presenters to be included through virtual conferencing techniques to increase the target audience. A further recommendation is to develop a set of good practices for hosting Side Events, such as how to identify partners, draft a dynamic agenda and generate dialogue among the audience. This might increase the quality and level of interaction among different stakeholders. These suggestions point to interesting and fruitful ways of better interconnecting the formal and informal spaces at the COP in the future.
